title-group.article-title: Efficacy and Safety of Semaglutide for Managing Antipsychotic-associated Weight Gain: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

abstract.p: Antipsychotic medication-induced weight gain (AIWG) is a difficult-to-manage condition. Semaglutide is a widely used weight-lowering agent, but its role in AIWG has been evaluated in only few studies. This SRM evaluated if semaglutide can be effectively and safely used for AIWG in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric diseases. Electronic databases were searched for articles evaluating the use of semaglutide for managing AIWG. The primary outcome was reduction in body weight. Secondary outcomes were changes in body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), HBA1c, metabolic parameters, and adverse events. Data from nine studies (44,233 participants; 4.21% diabetes; 94.79% euglycemia) which fulfilled all criteria were analysed. Semaglutide for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in weight [mean difference (MD) -7.37 kg (95% confidence interval (CI): -12.39, -2.35); P < 0.001; I2 = 99%], BMI [MD -2.76 kg/m2 (95% CI: -4.15, -1.37); P < 0.001; I2 = 98%], WC [MD -5.12 cm (95% CI: -7.21, -3.03); P < 0.001; I2 = 76%], HbA1c [MD -0.35% (95% CI: -0.47, -0.24); P < 0.001; I2 = 91%] and higher >5% weight loss [OR 2.25 (95% CI: 2.14, 2.36); P < 0.001; I2 = 0%]. The occurrence of nausea, diarrhoea, and injection site reactions was similar. Vomiting was significantly higher in semaglutide users. The occurrence of psychiatric adverse events was lower in semaglutide users but not significant [OR 0.59 (95% CI: 0.33–1.07); P = 0.08; I2 = 0%]. Semaglutide has good efficacy data with regard to quantum of weight loss with good safety for managing AIWG.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Antipsychotic medication-induced weight gain (AIWG), poor diet and lifestyle, and its sequelae like diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension significantly contribute to cardiovascular morbidity, medication compliance, and quality of life in people living with psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia.[1] Few studies and systematic reviews have evaluated the role of non-pharmacological interventions in AIWG with limited success.[23456] The landscape of obesity management has been dramatically redefined with the availability of newer glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) such as semaglutide. Older GLP1RAs, such as exenatide, dulaglutide, and lixisenatide, are primarily recommended for glycaemic control, although higher doses of liraglutide have been approved for weight management.[7] Of note, most GLP1RA trials have excluded individuals with mental illness such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorders, and other conditions necessitating antipsychotic medications. Emerging studies have shown the efficacy of these drugs in AIWG. A recent trial in clozapine/olanzapine-treated patients demonstrated 5.3 kg greater weight loss with liraglutide compared to placebo.[8] Meta-analyses confirm significant weight reductions (3–4 kg vs controls) and metabolic benefits with GLP1RAs, without worsening mental health.[9]

Among currently available GLP1RAs, semaglutide has the most robust weight reduction data in individuals with obesity and diabetes.[10] Literature search revealed that none of the systematic review or meta-analysis (SRM) has analysed the efficacy and safety of semaglutide for AIWG. The present study aims to bridge this knowledge gap. This SRM aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of semaglutide for managing AIWG in individuals with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric disorders.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: This SRM was conducted according to the procedures outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions[11] and is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist.[12]

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: Several databases and registers were systematically searched (Cochrane, ISI web of science, PubMed, and Scopus). The search spanned these sources from their inception to 31 December 2025. Using the Boolean operators ‘AND’ and ‘OR’, the following terms were searched: ‘semaglutide’, ‘GLP-1 receptor agonists’, and ‘schizophrenia’, ‘bipolar disorder’, ‘psychiatric disorders’, ‘antipsychotic medicine’, ‘antipsychotic induced weight gain’. The search terms targeted titles, abstracts, and keywords to identify published studies in the English language. The details of the search strategies are shown in Table 1. Furthermore, the process involved examining the references cited in the articles obtained for this research as well as relevant journals.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The population, intervention, controls, outcomes, and study design served as the framework for establishing eligibility criteria for the clinical trials in this SRM. The patient population (P) consisted of individuals (≥18 years) diagnosed with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or other psychiatric disorder with body mass index (BMI) more than 27 kg/m2 and use of antipsychotic medications for at least three months. The intervention (I) was oral or injectable semaglutide for at least 12 weeks. The comparison or control (C) included adults receiving either a placebo or any other approved medication for AIWG. The outcomes (O) included the mean change in body weight (kg), mean change in BMI, waist circumference (WC), HbA1c, and adverse events. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized prospective studies, retrospective cohort studies, and single-arm studies with a duration of at least 12 weeks were considered as the study type (S) for inclusion. Clinical trials involving animals or healthy humans, pooled analyses of clinical trials, conference proceedings, preprints, letters to the editor, case reports, and articles that did not provide data on outcomes of interest were excluded from consideration.

sec.title: Outcomes analysed
sec.p: The primary outcome of interest is the mean reduction in body weight from baseline following treatment with semaglutide. Secondary outcomes of interest include mean change in BMI, WC, HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipid parameters, body composition parameters, and side effect profile.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the identified studies. They reviewed the full text to determine if a study could not be excluded based solely on the title and abstract. Any disagreements concerning the study’s eligibility were resolved by consulting a third author.

sec.title: Data extraction and dealing with missing data
sec.p: Four review authors independently performed data extraction, utilizing standardized forms. The following data were extracted for all eligible studies and included in the review: first author, year of publication, country where the study was conducted, study design, major inclusion criteria for study subjects, sample size, mean age, BMI, concomitant medications, and trial duration. Additionally, as previously mentioned, data on primary and secondary outcomes were extracted. All disagreements were settled through consensus.

sec.title: Data synthesis and statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were presented as mean/standard deviation, whereas categorical variables were presented as frequency/proportion. The outcomes were measured as mean differences (MD) for the continuous variables and odds ratios (OR) or risk ratios (RR) for the categorical variables, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). For the studies with a non-semaglutide control group, the MDs for the changes from baseline values of the continuous outcomes in the semaglutide versus control groups; OR for the categorical variables were calculated using the Review Manager online software (RevMan Web) version 9.14.0 (Cochrane Collaboration UK, 2025). For the single-arm studies using semaglutide only, the mean changes from baseline values of the continuous outcomes were pooled to generate the effect sizes using the ‘meta’ and ‘metafor’ packages in RStudio for R Statistics programming (version 2025.4.5.0) for the single-arm meta-analysis.[13]

The random-effects model was chosen to address the anticipated heterogeneity resulting from population characteristics in the included studies. The inverse variance statistical method was applied for all instances. Details of the meta-analysis included using the restricted maximum-likelihood estimator for tau2, the Q-profile method for CI of tau2 and tau. Calculation of I2 was based on Q statistics using untransformed (raw) means. Forest plots were generated with the same software. Forest plots were generated for visualization in RStudio.

sec.title: Assessment of heterogeneity and publication bias
sec.p: The assessment of heterogeneity was initially performed by examining forest plots. Subsequently, Chi-squared tests were conducted using N-1 degrees of freedom and a significance level of 0.05 to assess statistical significance. The I2 test was also used in the subsequent analysis. Thresholds for I² values were defined as follows: 25% for low heterogeneity, 50% for moderate heterogeneity, and 75% for high heterogeneity.[13]

sec.title: Assessment of the quality of the included studies
sec.p: Two authors independently evaluated the risk of bias in the included studies using the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions, version 2 (ROBINS-I V2) for the RCTs and non-randomized intervention trials.[14] The ROBINS-I V2 tool covers seven domains through which bias might be introduced. Based on these responses to the signalling questions, which aim to elicit information relevant to the RoB judgment for the domain, the options for a domain-level RoB judgment are ‘Low’, ‘Moderate’, ‘Serious’, or ‘Critical’ risk of bias, with an additional option of ‘No information’. The judgments within each domain are carried forward to an overall RoB judgment across bias domains for the outcome being assessed. In discrepancies, the sixth and seventh authors acted as arbitrators to achieve consensus. The Risk-of-bias VISualization (robvis) web app was used to create risk-of-bias plots.[151617] The Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, version 2 (ROB2), was used to assess potential biases in RCTs, concentrating on key areas such as randomization procedures, deviations from intended interventions, incomplete outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selective reporting.[16]

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: A total of 445 articles were found on initial review. The details of the search are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. One hundred and thirteen duplicates were removed. Following the review of the title and abstracts, the search was narrowed down to nine articles (three RCTs, three case–control/cohort studies, and three single-arm studies), which fulfilled all the inclusion and exclusion criteria were analysed in this SRM.[181920212223242526] The details of the patient characteristics of the nine studies analysed in this SRM have been elaborated in Table 2. Data from a total of 44,233 patients with AIWG (4.21% with diabetes; 1% with prediabetes, and remaining with euglycemia) were analysed. The majority of the study participants were undergoing treatment for schizophrenia or related disorders [Table 2]. Injectable semaglutide was used for treatment in eight out of the nine studies analysed with the duration of therapy ranging from two months to 12 months [Table 2]. In the study by Varghese et al.[26] 88.31% patients were on semaglutide, and 11.69% patients were on tirzepatide.[26] Data from patients on semaglutide were analysed. The details of the specific antipsychotic medications received by patients are shown in Table 2.

sec.title: Risk if bias and quality assessment of the analysed studies
sec.p: The ROBINS-I V2 risk of bias for all the studies analysed was low and is shown in Supplementary Figure 1a. Risk of bias assessment in RCTs was done using ROB2 and was low [Supplementary Figure 1b]. Publication bias assessment was not performed due to the presence of fewer than 10 RCTs in the forest plots.[27]

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: Data from five studies (43,771 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on weight reduction in people with AIWG. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in body weight as compared to controls [MD -7.37 kg (95% CI: -12.39, -2.35); P < 0.001; I2 = 99% (considerable heterogeneity); Figure 2a]. However, the significance was blunted on prediction interval analysis due to data heterogeneity [CI: -19.57, 4.83 kg]

caption.p: Forest plot highlighting the impact of semaglutide therapy as compared to controls in people with antipsychotic medication-induced weight gain on (a): Body weight; (b): Body mass index (BMI); (c): Waist circumference (WC); (d): >5% weight loss; (e): Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c); (f): Fasting glucose; (g): Systolic blood pressure (SBP); (h): Diastolic blood pressure (DBP)

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: Data from five studies (355 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on BMI in people with AIWG. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in BMI as compared to controls [MD -2.76 kg/m2 (95% CI: -4.15, -1.37); P < 0.001; I2 = 98% (considerable heterogeneity); Figure 2b]. However, the significance was blunted on prediction interval analysis due to data heterogeneity [CI: -6.04, 0.52 kg/m2]. Data from three studies (262 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on WC in people with AIWG. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in WC as compared to controls [MD -5.12 cm (95% CI: -7.21, -3.03); P < 0.001; I2 = 76% (considerable heterogeneity); Figure 2c], which persisted on prediction interval analysis. Data from two studies (43,540 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on chances of achieving > 5% weight loss from baseline. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significantly higher chances of > 5% weight loss as compared to controls [OR 2.25 (95% CI: 2.14, 2.36); P < 0.001; I2 = 0% (low heterogeneity); Figure 2d].

Data from five studies (355 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on HbA1c in people with AIWG. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in HbA1c as compared to controls [MD -0.35% (95% CI: -0.47, -0.24); P < 0.001; I2 = 91% (considerable heterogeneity); Figure 2e], which persisted on prediction interval analysis. Data from three studies (140 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on fasting glucose in people with AIWG. Semaglutide therapy for AIWG was associated with a significant reduction in fasting glucose as compared to controls [MD -5.93 mg/dl (95% CI: -7.80, -4.06); P < 0.001; I2 = 8% (low heterogeneity); Figure 2f]. Data from three studies (140 patients) were analysed to find the impact of semaglutide therapy on systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) in people with AIWG. SBP [MD -1.52 mm Hg (95% CI: -3.08, 0.04); P = 0.06; I2 = 0% (low heterogeneity); Figure 2g] and DBP [MD 1.00 mm Hg (95% CI: -0.69, 2.69); P = 0.25; I2 = 63% (low heterogeneity); Figure 2h] were comparable in patients who received semaglutide as compared to controls.

sec.title: Safety profile
sec.p: The occurrence of TAEs was similar in patients receiving semaglutide as compared to controls [OR 1.19 (95% CI: 0.7–2.02); P = 0.52; I2 = 0%; Figure 3a]. The occurrence of SAEs was similar in patients receiving semaglutide as compared to controls [OR 0.60 (95% CI: 0.25–1.44); P = 0.25; I2 = 0%; Figure 3b]. The occurrence of nausea was higher in patients on semaglutide as compared to controls [OR 2.10 (95% CI: 1.11–4.00); P = 0.02; I2 = 20%; Figure 3c], but lost its significance on prediction interval analysis due to data heterogeneity. The occurrence of vomiting was significantly higher in patients on semaglutide as compared to controls [OR 2.95 (95% CI: 1.45–6.00); P = 0.003; I2 = 0%; Figure 3d]. The occurrence of diarrhoea [OR 1.33 (95% CI: 0.57–3.13); P = 0.51; I2 = 19%; Figure 3e] and injection site reactions [OR 0.94 (95% CI: 0.43–2.04); P = 0.87; I2 = 0%; Figure 3f] were similar in patients on semaglutide as compared to controls. The occurrence of psychiatric adverse events was lower in patients on semaglutide as compared to controls, but statistically not significant [OR 0.59 (95% CI: 0.33–1.07); P = 0.08; I2 = 0%; Figure 3g]. The occurrence of suicidal attempt/ideation was similar in patients on semaglutide as compared to controls [OR 0.78 (95% CI: 0.08–7.28); P = 0.83; I2 = 25%; Figure 3h].

sec.p: The occurrence of abdominal pain and constipation was not significantly different among those receiving semaglutide as compared to controls [Table 3]. Serum triglycerides and LDL-C were similar in patients receiving semaglutide as compared to controls [Table 3]. There was a significant reduction in total body fat and visceral fat in patients receiving semaglutide as compared to controls [Table 3].

sec.title: Key outcomes of use of semaglutide for AIWG in single-arm studies
sec.p: In two single-arm real-world studies (Prasad et al., 2023[22]; Heald et al., 2025[23]), semaglutide therapy resulted in a pooled mean weight reduction of -6.15 kg [MD -6.15 kg (95% CI: –20.15, 7.84); P = 0.27; I² =17.9%)]. However, the 95% CI was wide (–20.15, 7.84 kg) due to small sample size, though heterogeneity was low. Both studies showed improvement in glycaemic parameters with acceptable tolerability. The summary of the key outcomes of use of semaglutide for AIWG in single-arm studies is shown in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Schizophrenia and other severe mental illnesses are associated with adverse metabolic profiles and increased cardiovascular mortality. The cardiovascular mortality rate is two to three times higher than in the general population, with an estimated 15–20-year reduction in life expectancy.[1] Antipsychotics contribute to weight gain through different mechanisms which include metabolic dysregulation, appetite modulation, and hormonal changes.[28] Semaglutide, apart from its delayed gastric emptying mechanism, through direct impact on the central nervous system, especially on satiety centres, on neuropeptides related to appetite regulation can help in managing AIWG.[28]

Numerous pharmacological interventions have been tried in management of AIWG. Metformin is the most studied intervention which has shown mild weight loss (around 1-3 kg) with some improvement in insulin resistance in individuals with schizophrenia compared to placebo.[3] Topiramate has also shown some benefit; however, cognitive side effects limit its use.[4] Other agents have shown lesser promise, with sibutramine withdrawn for cardiotoxicity and reboxetine showing mild efficacy.[56] This SRM highlights that semaglutide, which is approved for the treatment of diabetes and obesity, with strong evidence of improving cardiovascular and renal outcomes, is an effective medicine for managing AIWG in people living with psychiatric disorders.

People living with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric disorders on antipsychotic medications on an average lost 7.4 kg weight following six to 12 months of semaglutide use, along with a significant reduction in central obesity (>5 m decline in WC). Gastrointestinal problems were the predominant side effects noted, as has been previously reported in all the trials and real-world studies.

The results from this SRM suggests that semaglutide may be better than other medications tried previously for AIWG. Metformin, the most widely studied drug in this setting, typically produces weight loss of 2–3 kg over 12–24 weeks, with ~20–25% patients achieving ≥5% weight loss.[19] Other drugs, like topiramate, have demonstrated 2–4 kg reduction in weight with poor tolerability profile and cognitive adverse effects.[29] Among the other GLP1RAs, exenatide reported a mean weight loss of − 2.48 kg and a mean BMI reduction of − 0.82%. Liraglutide (high dose) in contrast demonstrated a mean weight loss of − 4.70 kg and a BMI reduction of − 1.52%.[30] Two systematic reviews have evaluated weight loss in individuals with schizophrenia treated with agents such as metformin, naltrexone–bupropion, topiramate–phentermine, dulaglutide, liraglutide, or exenatide, with only modest reductions observed.[3132]

The Semaglutide Treatment Effect for People with obesity (STEP) 1–5 trials evaluated the impact of semaglutide in managing obesity.[33] They excluded individuals with underlying psychiatric disorders on antipsychotic medications, but included patients in anti-depressants for depression.[31] Post hoc analysis of subgroup of participants on anti-depressants showed on an average 15.7% weight loss from baseline over 68 weeks of therapy.[33] Previous meta-analysis has noted on an average 11.49% weight loss with semaglutide in people with obesity.[34] Hence, the weight reduction achieved with semaglutide in AIWG appears lower than that observed in individuals without psychiatric disorder.

No new safety signals with regard to the use of semaglutide for AIWG from this SRM are reassuring. Semaglutide does not have any psychiatric warnings in labelling.[35] Analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) data, which albeit has its own share of bias, identified significant depression and suicidality signals with semaglutide in weight management.[35] Post hoc analysis of the STEP clinical trials data for the psychiatric safety of semaglutide for weight management in people without known major psychopathology showed that treatment with semaglutide, 2.4 mg, did not increase the risk of developing symptoms of depression or suicidal behaviour and was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms.[36]

A major strength of this SRM is its focus on semaglutide for antipsychotic medication-induced weight gain, a population that has been under-represented in obesity and diabetes clinical trials. It is reassuring to see that there was no increase, in fact a trend towards decreased occurrence of psychiatric adverse events when semaglutide was used for AIWG. The current study is subject to few important limitations. There is variability in diagnosis of psychiatric illness, duration and as well as category of antipsychotic drug used. Another limitation of this SRM is the relative short duration of semaglutide therapy in the studies analysed. The median duration of semaglutide therapy was six months. Hence, further studies with a longer duration of follow-up are needed to establish the durability of weight loss with the use of semaglutide for AIWG. Sass et al.[37] are doing a 26 week, double-blinded placebo controlled, randomized, parallel-group RCT evaluating the impact of semaglutide on dysglycaemia in patients on clozapine-treated or olanzapine-treated patients diagnosed with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SemaPsychiatry study). The results of this RCT are expected by next year and are likely to add vital evidence.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Given that individuals on antipsychotic therapy are systematically excluded from major large-scale trials, our findings provide reassuring efficacy and safety data on the use for semaglutide for managing AIWG. Semaglutide has good efficacy data with regard to the quantum of weight loss with good safety for managing AIWG; however, the quantum of weight loss is still lesser as compared to patients not on antipsychotic medications.
